phy_ocra.1.0.summary: When a substance **melts, freezes, evaporates, condenses or sublimates**, its mass stays exactly the same, because the number of particles does not change: they are only rearranged and spaced differently. These changes of state are **physical changes**, which differ from chemical changes because if the change is reversed the material **recovers its original properties**. Any apparent loss of mass, for example when water boils in an open pan, is because particles escape from an open system, not because mass is destroyed.

core.p: A change of state is when a substance changes between solid, liquid and gas. You need to know the name of each change and its reverse. Every one of them is a physical change.
bullets: **Melting**: solid to liquid
**Freezing**: liquid to solid (the reverse of melting)
**Evaporating / boiling**: liquid to gas
**Condensing**: gas to liquid (the reverse of evaporating)
**Sublimating**: solid straight to gas without becoming a liquid (e.g. dry ice, solid carbon dioxide)
The reverse of sublimation (gas straight to solid) is called **deposition**

core.p: In a change of state, no particles are created and none are destroyed. The same particles are simply arranged differently and move differently. Because the mass of a sample is the total mass of all its particles, and the number and type of particles do not change, the mass does not change.
bullets: **Mass is conserved** in melting, freezing, evaporating, condensing and sublimating
The **number of particles stays the same**
The particles themselves **do not change**: water molecules are still water molecules in ice, water and steam
Only the **arrangement, spacing and movement** of the particles change
100 g of ice melts to give **exactly 100 g of water**

callouts.p: The particles are not created or destroyed, only rearranged, so the total mass stays the same.

core.h: What does change in a change of state
core.p: Although the mass stays the same, other things do change. This is a favourite exam contrast: students must separate mass (conserved) from volume and density (which change).
bullets: **Spacing** between particles changes (far apart in a gas, touching in solids and liquids)
**Volume** changes, usually increasing a lot on boiling
**Density** changes, because density = mass / volume and the volume changes while the mass does not
The **energy stored** in the system (internal energy) changes, because heating or cooling is needed
The **forces / bonds between particles** are overcome or form, but the particles themselves are unchanged

callouts.p: Steam takes up far more space than the water it came from, but it does not have more mass.

core.h: Showing conservation of mass in the lab
core.p: You can show that mass is conserved by measuring the mass of a sample before and after a change of state, making sure nothing can get in or out. A classic demonstration is melting ice in a container on a balance.
bullets: Place ice in a beaker on a **zeroed top-pan balance** and record the mass
Leave the ice to **melt** and record the mass again
The reading is **the same** (within the resolution of the balance)
Cover the beaker so water does not **evaporate** and escape during the experiment
Wipe the outside dry: **condensation** from the air on a cold beaker would add mass that was not part of the sample

callouts.p: If an exam says the mass went up slightly, suggest water vapour from the air condensed on the cold beaker; if it went down, suggest some water evaporated.

core.p: Mass is always conserved, but you only measure it as unchanged if the system is closed. In an open system particles can escape (or enter), so the measured mass can change even though no mass has been destroyed.
bullets: **Closed system**: nothing can enter or leave, so the measured mass stays the same
**Open system**: particles can enter or leave
Boiling water in an open pan: the mass of the pan **decreases** because **water vapour escapes** into the air, not because mass is destroyed
A puddle drying up: the water has **evaporated into the air**; the mass is still there as water vapour
If the steam were collected and condensed, you would get back the **same mass of water**

callouts.p: Never write that water is used up or destroyed when it boils. It has changed state and left the open container as a gas.

core.p: A physical change does not make a new substance. Because the particles are unchanged, you can reverse the change and get back the original material with all its original properties. Melting ice gives water; freezing that water gives ice that is identical to the original ice.
bullets: Changes of state are **physical changes**
**No new substance** is formed
The change can be **reversed** by cooling instead of heating (or heating instead of cooling)
When reversed, the material **recovers its original properties**: same melting point, same density, same colour, same chemical behaviour
Example: wax melts when heated and becomes solid wax again when cooled
Example: water evaporates and condenses back to water

callouts.p: A change in which no new substance is made; the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.

core.h: How physical changes differ from chemical changes
core.p: In a chemical change, atoms are rearranged into new substances with different properties. Even if you try to reverse the conditions, you do not simply get the original material back. Burning wood, cooking an egg and rusting iron are chemical changes.
bullets: Chemical change: **new substance(s)** formed
Chemical change: bonds within particles break and **atoms rearrange**
Chemical change: usually **not easily reversed**; cooling ash does not give wood
Physical change: same particles, just **rearranged or spaced differently**
Physical change: reversing it gives back the **original material with its original properties**

callouts.p: Changes of state differ from chemical changes because the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.

core.p: Grade 9 answers explain conservation of mass and reversibility using particles, not just by stating them. The same particles are present before and after; heating gives them energy to overcome the forces between them, and cooling lets the forces pull them back together.
bullets: Melting: particles gain energy, **break free of fixed positions**, but stay touching
Boiling / evaporating: particles gain enough energy to **overcome the forces** and move far apart
Condensing and freezing: particles lose energy, the **attractive forces pull them closer** and into fixed positions
At every stage the **same particles** are present, so mass is unchanged
Because the particles are unchanged, reversing the energy transfer **restores the original arrangement and properties**

core.p: Some substances change directly from a solid to a gas without becoming a liquid. This is still a physical change and mass is still conserved.
bullets: Example: **solid carbon dioxide (dry ice)** sublimates at room pressure
Example: **iodine** crystals sublimate when heated gently
Cooling the gas can turn it straight back to solid (deposition), recovering the original solid
Frost forming on a cold night is water vapour depositing as ice
The mass of gas produced equals the **mass of solid** that sublimated

core.h: Mass, volume and density in a change of state
core.p: Because mass is conserved but volume changes, you can work out a new volume or density after a change of state using density = mass / volume. This links to P1.1 density.
bullets: Mass before = **mass after**
New volume = mass / new density
Water: 1000 kg/m³; ice: about 920 kg/m³, so **ice has a larger volume** than the same mass of water
That is why water pipes can **burst when they freeze**
Gases have a very large volume for the same mass, so **very low density**

callouts.p: Find the mass from the first state using m = ρ × V, then use that same mass with the second density.

core.p: Mark schemes reward specific phrases. Use them precisely.
bullets: Say **mass is conserved** (or stays the same), not weight is lost
Say **the number of particles stays the same**
Say **particles are not created or destroyed**
Say the material **recovers its original properties** when the change is reversed
Say water vapour **escapes from an open container**
Name the change of state correctly: melting, freezing, evaporating / boiling, condensing, sublimating

analogy.p: Think of a substance as a set of 100 Lego bricks. A neat solid wall, a loose heap and bricks scattered across the floor are three different arrangements, but you still have exactly 100 bricks with the same total mass: that is a change of state. Scoop them up and rebuild the wall and it is the same wall as before, which is why physical changes are reversible. A chemical change is like melting the bricks down and moulding them into a different toy: you cannot just snap the original wall back together. Where it breaks down: real particles are not glued into place by studs, they are held by attractive forces, and in a gas they move continuously and fill their container.

terms.d: A change between solid, liquid and gas, e.g. melting or condensing; a physical change.
Change from solid to liquid.
Change from liquid to solid.
Change from liquid to gas, at the surface of a liquid at any temperature.
Change from liquid to gas throughout the liquid at its boiling point.
Change from gas to liquid.
Change directly from solid to gas without becoming a liquid.
Change directly from gas to solid; the reverse of sublimation.
The total mass stays the same during a change because particles are not created or destroyed.
A change where no new substance forms and the material recovers its original properties when the change is reversed.
A change in which new substances with different properties are formed.
Able to be undone so that the original material is recovered.
A system that no matter can enter or leave, so its total mass stays constant.
A system that matter can enter or leave, e.g. an uncovered beaker.
A tiny piece of matter (atom or molecule) making up a substance.
A characteristic of a material, such as melting point, density or colour.

mistakes.w: Water loses mass when it turns to steam.
mistakes.r: Mass is conserved; in an open container the steam escapes so the measured mass falls.

mistakes.w: Steam has more mass because it takes up more space.
mistakes.r: Volume increases but mass stays the same, so density decreases.

mistakes.w: The particles get bigger when a substance boils.
mistakes.r: Particles stay the same size; they move further apart.

mistakes.w: Melting is a chemical change because the substance looks different.
mistakes.r: Melting is a physical change: no new substance forms and it can be reversed.

mistakes.w: Physical changes are reversible because they need little energy.
mistakes.r: They are reversible because the particles are unchanged, so reversing the change recovers the original material and properties.

mistakes.w: Evaporation destroys the water.
mistakes.r: The water particles leave as water vapour; they still exist and still have mass.

mistakes.w: Sublimation means a gas turning into a liquid.
mistakes.r: Sublimation is solid turning directly to gas.

mistakes.w: New particles are made when ice melts.
mistakes.r: The same particles are present; only their arrangement and movement change.

exam.q: State what happens to the mass of a block of ice when it melts.
model: The mass stays the same / is conserved
exam.tip: One word answers like same are fine if clear.

exam.q: Name the change of state from gas to liquid.
model: Condensing / condensation
exam.tip: Spell the term correctly; do not confuse with evaporating.

exam.q: Explain why mass is conserved when water freezes.
model: The number of particles stays the same / particles are not created or destroyed
The particles are only rearranged into fixed positions
exam.tip: Give the particle reason, not just a restatement.

exam.q: A student heats 200 g of water in an open beaker until some boils. The mass falls to 170 g. Explain why, and state what has happened to the missing 30 g.
model: Water has evaporated / boiled and the water vapour has escaped from the open beaker
The 30 g still exists as water vapour in the air; mass has not been destroyed
exam.tip: Mention the system is open.

exam.q: Describe how a student could show that mass is conserved when ice melts.
model: Put ice in a covered container on a zeroed balance and record the mass
Allow the ice to melt completely
Record the mass again
The two readings are the same, showing mass is conserved (keep the container covered and dry the outside)
exam.tip: Include a control on evaporation or condensation for full marks.

exam.q: Explain how changes of state differ from chemical changes.
model: In a change of state no new substance is formed
If the change is reversed, the material recovers its original properties (in a chemical change new substances form and the change is not easily reversed)
exam.tip: Use the OCR phrase recovers its original properties.

exam.q: Classify each as physical or chemical: chocolate melting; toast burning; iodine sublimating.
model: Chocolate melting: physical
Toast burning: chemical
Iodine sublimating: physical
exam.tip: Ask: is a new substance formed?

exam.q: 0.5 kg of water freezes. Ice has a density of 920 kg/m³. Calculate the volume of the ice.
model: Mass of ice = 0.5 kg (mass is conserved)
exam.tip: The first mark is for recognising the mass does not change.

exam.q: Using the particle model, explain why boiling increases the volume of a substance but not its mass.
model: Particles gain energy and overcome the forces between them
Particles move far apart, so the volume increases
The number (and type) of particles is unchanged
So the mass is unchanged, and density decreases
exam.tip: Separate the volume reasoning from the mass reasoning.

exam.q: Explain, with reference to particles and properties, why melting wax and burning wax are different types of change. Include how you could test each.
model: Melting wax is a physical change / change of state
The wax particles stay the same; they are only rearranged and move more freely
Cooling the liquid wax gives solid wax with its original properties (e.g. same melting point, appearance)
Burning wax is a chemical change
New substances (e.g. carbon dioxide and water) are formed
These cannot be turned back into wax by cooling; mass is conserved in both if all products are kept in a closed system
exam.tip: Six-mark answers should compare both changes on the same points.

worked.q: A sealed bag contains 12 g of dry ice (solid carbon dioxide). It is left until all the dry ice has sublimated. What is the mass of carbon dioxide gas in the bag, and why does the bag swell?
steps: Sublimation is a change of state: solid to gas
The bag is sealed, so it is a closed system and no particles escape
The number of CO₂ particles is unchanged, so mass = 12 g
The particles are now far apart and moving fast, so the gas takes up a much larger volume and pushes the bag outwards
worked.ans: 12 g of carbon dioxide gas; the bag swells because the volume increases, not the mass.

worked.q: A water pipe contains 0.92 kg of water at 1000 kg/m³. It freezes to ice of density 920 kg/m³. Calculate the volume before and after freezing.
steps: Volume of water: V = m / ρ = 0.92 / 1000 = 0.00092 m³
Mass is conserved on freezing, so mass of ice = 0.92 kg
Volume of ice: V = 0.92 / 920 = 0.001 m³
Increase in volume = 0.001 − 0.00092 = 0.00008 m³
worked.ans: Water 0.00092 m³, ice 0.0010 m³: same mass, larger volume, which can burst the pipe.

worked.q: Model answer: A pan of soup is boiled with the lid off and loses 50 g. Then the experiment is repeated with a tightly fitting lid, and the mass does not change. Explain both results.
steps: Lid off: open system, water evaporates and the vapour escapes into the room, so the measured mass falls by 50 g
The 50 g has not been destroyed; it is water vapour in the air
Lid on: closed system, vapour condenses on the lid and drips back
No particles leave, so the mass is conserved and the reading stays constant
worked.ans: Mass is always conserved; it only appears to fall when vapour escapes from an open system.

phy_ocra.1.1.summary: Heating a system **transfers energy** to it and increases the **energy stored inside it (its internal energy)**. That extra energy does one of two things: it either **raises the temperature** of the system, by making its particles move faster, or it **changes the state** of the system, by letting particles overcome the forces between them, while the temperature stays constant. A heating curve shows both effects, with sloping sections where temperature rises and flat sections where the state changes.

core.p: In physics a system is the object or group of objects you are studying, such as a beaker of water or a block of ice. Energy can be stored in a system in different ways. When we heat a system, energy is transferred into its thermal (internal) store.
bullets: A **system** is an object or group of objects being studied
Heating is an **energy transfer** from a hotter object to a cooler one
Heating increases the **energy stored in the system**
The energy is stored by the **particles** of the system
Cooling is the reverse: energy is transferred **out of** the system to the surroundings

callouts.p: Heating a system increases its internal energy. This either raises its temperature or changes its state.

core.p: The energy stored inside a system by its particles is called its internal energy. Particles store energy in two ways: by moving (kinetic energy) and because of their positions relative to each other and the forces between them (potential energy).
bullets: **Internal energy** = total **kinetic energy + potential energy** of all the particles
**Kinetic energy**: due to the particles' motion (vibrating, moving around)
**Potential energy**: due to the forces / bonds between particles and how far apart they are
Heating increases internal energy
Internal energy depends on the **mass** of the system as well as its temperature and state

callouts.p: The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles (atoms and molecules) that make up a system.

fig.cap: Particles store internal energy in two ways: kinetic energy because they move, and potential energy because of the forces between them and their separation.

core.p: Temperature is linked to how fast the particles are moving. When the temperature of a substance rises, its particles move faster on average, so their average kinetic energy increases. A thermometer measures temperature, not internal energy.
bullets: Higher temperature means particles have **higher average kinetic energy**
In a solid, particles **vibrate faster** about fixed positions
In a liquid or gas, particles **move around faster**
Temperature is measured in **°C** (or kelvin, K)
Temperature is **not the same as internal energy**: a bath of warm water has more internal energy than a cup of boiling water

callouts.p: Temperature tells you the average kinetic energy of the particles. Internal energy is the total energy of all the particles, so it also depends on how many particles (how much mass) there are.

core.p: When energy is transferred to a system by heating, the internal energy always increases. Where that energy goes decides what you observe: either the particles speed up (temperature rises) or the particles move apart and break free of each other (state changes).
bullets: Effect 1: **temperature rises**: energy increases the **kinetic energy** of the particles
Effect 2: **state changes** (melting or boiling): energy increases the **potential energy** of the particles as they overcome the forces between them
During a change of state the **temperature stays constant**
Which happens depends on whether the substance is **at its melting or boiling point**
Cooling does the opposite: temperature falls, or the substance condenses or freezes

core.p: If you heat ice at a steady rate and plot temperature against time, you get a heating curve. The sloping parts show the temperature rising within one state. The flat parts (plateaus) show a change of state, where energy is still going in but the temperature does not change.
bullets: **Sloping section**: one state only, temperature rising, particle kinetic energy increasing
**First plateau**: melting at the **melting point** (0 °C for ice)
**Second plateau**: boiling at the **boiling point** (100 °C for water)
On each plateau, energy is still being supplied and **internal energy is still increasing**
The boiling plateau is usually **longer** than the melting plateau because more energy is needed to separate particles completely into a gas
The gradient of a sloping section depends on the substance and its mass

callouts.p: Flat line = change of state at constant temperature. Sloping line = temperature change in a single state. Label both on any sketch.

core.h: Why temperature stays constant during a change of state
core.p: During melting or boiling, the energy supplied is used to overcome the forces of attraction between particles rather than to make them move faster. The average kinetic energy of the particles stays the same, so the temperature stays the same, but the potential energy of the particles increases, so the internal energy still rises.
bullets: Energy is used to **break / overcome the bonds (forces) between particles**
**Potential energy** of particles increases
**Average kinetic energy stays constant**, so temperature is constant
**Internal energy still increases**
The energy needed to change state without a change of temperature is called **latent heat** (calculations are covered in P1.2f)

callouts.p: Do not say no energy is being transferred on the flat section. Energy is still being supplied; it is changing the state, not the temperature.

core.p: When a system cools, energy is transferred from it to the surroundings and its internal energy decreases. A cooling curve is the mirror image of a heating curve, with plateaus where the substance condenses or freezes.
bullets: Cooling **decreases internal energy**
Sloping sections: temperature falls, particles **slow down**
Plateau when **condensing** or **freezing**: temperature constant
On the plateau, forces between particles pull them together and **energy is released** to the surroundings
This is why freezing water releases energy even though its temperature stays at 0 °C

core.p: For the same amount of energy supplied, the temperature rise of a system is not always the same. This links forward to specific heat capacity (P1.2d-e).
bullets: **Energy supplied**: more energy gives a bigger temperature rise
**Mass**: a larger mass shares the energy among more particles, so a **smaller temperature rise**
**Material**: different substances need different amounts of energy to warm up (different specific heat capacities)
Example: 1 kg of water needs much more energy to warm by 1 °C than 1 kg of copper

core.p: Two systems at the same temperature can have very different internal energies. Internal energy is the total for all the particles, so a bigger mass at the same temperature has more internal energy.
bullets: Swimming pool at 25 °C has **far more internal energy** than a cup of tea at 80 °C
Because the pool has **vastly more particles**
Temperature is about the **average** kinetic energy per particle
Internal energy is about the **total** energy of all particles
Ice at 0 °C and water at 0 °C have the same temperature, but the **water has more internal energy** (higher potential energy)

head: Temperature
Internal energy
rows: Total KE + PE of all particles

core.p: Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid at any temperature, not only at the boiling point. The fastest-moving particles have enough energy to escape. This leaves the slower particles behind, so the average kinetic energy of the remaining liquid falls and it cools.
bullets: Only the **most energetic particles** escape from the surface
The **average kinetic energy** of the particles left behind falls
So the **temperature of the liquid decreases**
Example: **sweating** cools you down as sweat evaporates
Evaporation is faster when the liquid is warmer, has a larger surface area or air moves over it

core.p: Precise wording earns the marks on this point.
bullets: Heating **transfers energy to the system** / increases its **internal energy**
Internal energy = **kinetic + potential** energy of the particles
Temperature rise: particles **move (vibrate) faster**, kinetic energy increases
Change of state: energy **overcomes forces / breaks bonds between particles**, potential energy increases
**Temperature remains constant** during a change of state
Say **energy**, not heat, when describing what is stored

analogy.p: Picture the particles as dancers holding hands. Turning up the music (heating) gives them more energy. At first they just dance faster on the spot or around the floor: that is the temperature rising, because their movement energy goes up. At a certain point, extra energy stops making them dance faster and is used instead to let go of each other's hands and spread out across a bigger room: that is a change of state, with the same dance speed (temperature) but more energy stored in the broken links. Where it breaks down: real particles do not choose when to let go; it happens at a fixed melting or boiling point, and the energy is stored as potential energy due to forces, not as a decision.

terms.d: An object or group of objects being studied.
Energy transfer from a hotter object to a cooler one because of a temperature difference.
The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles in a system.
Energy particles have because they are moving or vibrating.
Energy particles have due to the forces between them and their separation.
A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance.
A change between solid, liquid and gas, which happens at constant temperature.
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid.
The temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas throughout its volume.
Graph of temperature against time as a substance is heated at a steady rate.
Graph of temperature against time as a substance cools.
Flat section of a heating or cooling curve showing a change of state at constant temperature.
Energy needed to change the state of a substance without changing its temperature.
Liquid turning to gas at the surface, at temperatures below the boiling point.
When objects are at the same temperature, so there is no net energy transfer by heating between them.

mistakes.w: During melting no energy is being supplied because the temperature does not change.
mistakes.r: Energy is still supplied; it increases the potential energy of the particles by overcoming forces between them.

mistakes.w: Temperature and internal energy are the same thing.
mistakes.r: Temperature relates to average particle kinetic energy; internal energy is the total KE + PE of all particles.

mistakes.w: Heating always makes the temperature rise.
mistakes.r: Heating either raises the temperature or changes the state.

mistakes.w: During boiling the particles get faster.
mistakes.r: During boiling the average kinetic energy stays the same; the energy separates the particles (potential energy increases).

mistakes.w: Particles expand when heated.
mistakes.r: Particles move faster and further apart; the particles themselves do not get bigger.

mistakes.w: Internal energy is just the kinetic energy of the particles.
mistakes.r: Internal energy includes both kinetic and potential energy of the particles.

mistakes.w: A cup of boiling water has more internal energy than a bath of warm water.
mistakes.r: The bath has more internal energy because it has far more particles.

mistakes.w: Heat is stored in the object.
mistakes.r: Energy is stored in the system's internal (thermal) store; heating is the transfer.

exam.q: State two ways that heating can change a system.
model: It can raise the temperature of the system
It can change the state of the system
exam.tip: Both effects come from an increase in internal energy.

exam.q: Define internal energy.
model: Total energy of the particles in a system
= kinetic energy + potential energy of all the particles
exam.tip: Mention both kinetic and potential.

exam.q: What happens to the motion of particles in a solid when its temperature increases?
model: They vibrate faster / with more energy about fixed positions
exam.tip: Say vibrate for a solid, not move around.

exam.q: On a heating curve, what is happening on the flat section at 100 °C for water?
model: The water is boiling / changing state from liquid to gas
Temperature stays constant while energy is still supplied
exam.tip: Give both the change and the constant temperature.

exam.q: Explain why the temperature of melting ice stays at 0 °C even though it is being heated.
model: Energy is used to break bonds / overcome forces between particles
This increases the potential energy of the particles (internal energy increases)
The average kinetic energy of the particles does not change, so temperature stays constant
exam.tip: Link each statement to particles.

exam.q: A swimming pool at 26 °C and a mug of coffee at 70 °C. Explain which has more internal energy.
model: The swimming pool
It has far more mass / particles, so the total kinetic and potential energy is greater, even though average kinetic energy is lower
exam.tip: Temperature is an average; internal energy is a total.

exam.q: Sketch and label a heating curve for a solid heated from below its melting point to above its boiling point.
model: Axes labelled temperature (y) and time (x)
Rising line for solid
Flat section labelled melting, then rising line for liquid
Flat section labelled boiling, then rising line for gas
exam.tip: Make the boiling plateau longer than the melting plateau.

exam.q: Explain why sweating helps to cool the body.
model: Sweat evaporates from the skin
The fastest / most energetic particles escape
Average kinetic energy of the remaining liquid falls so temperature falls, cooling the skin
exam.tip: Average kinetic energy is the key phrase.

exam.q: A beaker of water and a beaker of oil of equal mass are given the same energy. The oil gets hotter. Suggest why.
model: Different materials need different amounts of energy to raise their temperature
Oil has a lower specific heat capacity than water
exam.tip: This links to P1.2d; no calculation is needed.

exam.q: Describe, in terms of particles and energy, what happens as a block of ice at −10 °C is heated steadily until it becomes water at 20 °C.
model: Energy is transferred to the ice and its internal energy increases
From −10 °C to 0 °C particles vibrate faster; kinetic energy and temperature increase
At 0 °C the ice melts; temperature stays constant
Energy overcomes forces between particles; potential energy increases
After melting, particles in the liquid move faster; kinetic energy and temperature rise to 20 °C
Particles stay touching but in a random arrangement and can slide past each other
exam.tip: Work through each stage in time order, naming the energy store each time.

worked.q: Model answer: Use the heating curve of water to describe what happens to the internal energy, temperature and particles between the start of boiling and the end of boiling.
steps: Energy is supplied at a steady rate, so internal energy increases throughout
Temperature stays constant at 100 °C (the boiling point)
Average kinetic energy of the particles is constant
Energy is used to overcome the forces between particles so they move far apart
Potential energy of the particles increases
worked.ans: Internal energy rises, temperature stays at 100 °C, and the extra energy increases particle potential energy as liquid becomes gas.

worked.q: Applied example: Two identical pans contain 1 kg and 2 kg of water at 20 °C. Each receives the same energy from identical hobs for 2 minutes. Which reaches the higher temperature and why?
steps: Both systems receive the same energy, so both gain the same internal energy
In the 2 kg pan, the energy is shared among twice as many particles
So the average kinetic energy per particle increases less
The 2 kg pan has a smaller temperature rise
worked.ans: The 1 kg pan reaches the higher temperature, because the same energy is shared among fewer particles.

worked.q: Applied example: Explain why a freezer must keep removing energy from water at 0 °C to turn it into ice at 0 °C.
steps: Water at 0 °C and ice at 0 °C have the same temperature
Ice has lower internal energy because its particles have less potential energy (held in fixed positions)
When water freezes, attractive forces pull particles into fixed positions and energy is released
The freezer must transfer this energy away, otherwise freezing stops
worked.ans: Freezing lowers internal energy at constant temperature, so energy must be removed even though the temperature does not change.

phy_ocra.1.2.summary: **Specific heat capacity** is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C, and it explains why some materials heat up quickly while others, like water, warm up slowly. The amount of energy needed to change the temperature of a sample is calculated with **change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × change in temperature** (ΔE = m c Δθ). In PAG P5 you measure the specific heat capacity of a material by heating a known mass with an electrical heater, measuring the energy supplied and the temperature rise, and reducing energy losses with insulation.

core.p: Different materials need different amounts of energy to warm up by the same amount. Specific heat capacity is a property of a material that tells you how much energy it takes to raise the temperature of each kilogram by one degree. A material with a high specific heat capacity needs lots of energy to warm up and releases lots of energy as it cools.
bullets: **Specific** means per kilogram of the material
**Heat capacity** means how much energy it can take in per degree of temperature rise
Unit: **joules per kilogram per degree Celsius (J/kg°C)**
Water has a very high value: about **4200 J/kg°C**
Metals have low values (aluminium about 900 J/kg°C, copper about 390 J/kg°C), so they heat up and cool down quickly

core.p: The energy needed to change the temperature of a sample depends on three things: how much material there is (mass), what it is made of (specific heat capacity) and how much the temperature changes. OCR expects you to select and apply this equation.
bullets: **change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × change in temperature**
**ΔE = m × c × Δθ**
ΔE in **joules (J)**
m in **kilograms (kg)**
c in **J/kg°C**
Δθ in **°C** (a change of 1 °C is the same as a change of 1 K)
The same equation gives the energy **released** when a substance cools

callouts.p: change in thermal energy (J) = mass (kg) × specific heat capacity (J/kg°C) × change in temperature (°C)

core.p: Questions may ask for any one of the four quantities. Rearrange first, then substitute values in the correct units.
bullets: **ΔE = m × c × Δθ**
**c = ΔE / (m × Δθ)**
**m = ΔE / (c × Δθ)**
**Δθ = ΔE / (m × c)**
Δθ = **final temperature − initial temperature**
Final temperature = initial temperature + Δθ

callouts.p: If the question gives two temperatures, subtract them to find Δθ before substituting. Do not put the final temperature into the equation.

core.p: Most lost marks on this topic come from units, not physics.
bullets: Convert **grams to kilograms**: divide by 1000 (250 g = 0.25 kg)
Convert **kJ to J**: multiply by 1000 (8.4 kJ = 8400 J)
A temperature **change** in °C is numerically the same in K
Check your answer is sensible: heating a kettle of water takes hundreds of **kilojoules**
Give the unit J/kg°C when calculating c

callouts.p: Using mass in grams with c in J/kg°C makes the answer 1000 times too big.

core.h: Linking to internal energy and particles
core.p: When a substance is heated without changing state, the energy transferred increases the kinetic energy of its particles, so its temperature rises. Specific heat capacity tells you how much energy must be stored in the particles of 1 kg to raise the temperature by 1 °C.
bullets: Energy supplied increases the **internal energy** of the system
Without a change of state, this raises the **temperature**
**Larger mass**: energy shared among more particles, so smaller temperature rise
**Higher c**: more energy needed for each degree of rise
ΔE = m c Δθ only applies when there is **no change of state** (for changes of state use specific latent heat, P1.2f)

core.p: In PAG P5 you determine the specific heat capacity of a material, usually a metal block (such as aluminium) or water. An electrical heater supplies a measured amount of energy, and you measure the temperature rise of a known mass.
bullets: Measure the **mass** of the block with a top-pan balance (blocks are often 1 kg)
Place an **electrical immersion heater** in one hole and a **thermometer** in the other
Put a little **water or oil in the thermometer hole** to give good thermal contact
Wrap the block in **insulation** to reduce energy transfer to the surroundings
Record the **initial temperature**
Switch on the heater and measure the **energy supplied** with a joulemeter, or with an ammeter, voltmeter and stopwatch
Switch off after a set time (e.g. 10 minutes) and record the **highest temperature** reached
Calculate **c = ΔE / (m × Δθ)**

core.p: The energy supplied by the heater can be read directly from a joulemeter, or calculated from electrical measurements.
bullets: **Joulemeter**: reads energy in J directly (subtract the start reading from the end reading)
Or: measure **potential difference V** with a voltmeter in parallel with the heater
Measure **current I** with an ammeter in series
**Power P = V × I** (in watts)
**Energy E = P × t**, with t in **seconds**
So **E = V × I × t**

callouts.p: Time must be in seconds: 10 minutes = 600 s.

core.h: Using a graph to find c
core.p: A better method is to record the temperature at regular intervals (for example every minute) and plot temperature against energy supplied. The straight-line part of the graph has a gradient equal to 1 / (m × c), so c = 1 / (m × gradient).
bullets: Plot **temperature (y-axis) against energy supplied (x-axis)**
Draw a **line of best fit** through the straight section
**Gradient = Δθ / ΔE = 1 / (m × c)**
So **c = 1 / (m × gradient)**
Using a graph reduces the effect of **random errors** in single readings
The start of the graph may curve because the block takes time to warm up evenly

core.h: Errors and improvements in PAG P5
core.p: The measured value of c is usually higher than the accepted value. This is because some of the energy supplied is transferred to the surroundings instead of heating the block, so the temperature rise is smaller than it should be.
bullets: **Energy lost to the surroundings**: Δθ too small, so **c too large**
Reduce losses with **insulation** around the block (and a lid on top)
**Poor thermal contact** between heater, thermometer and block: put water or oil in the holes
**Thermometer lag**: the temperature keeps rising after the heater is switched off, so record the **highest temperature**
Some energy also heats the **heater and thermometer** themselves
Use a **digital thermometer / temperature probe** for higher resolution
**Repeat** and calculate a mean to reduce random error

callouts.p: Always say why the result is too high: less temperature rise for the energy measured, so c = ΔE / (m Δθ) is larger.

core.p: The heater and block get very hot, so the practical has clear hazards that exam questions sometimes ask about.
bullets: **Do not touch the heater or block** while hot; let it cool before handling
Stand the block on a **heat-proof mat**
Do not switch the heater on unless it is **inside the block** (it can overheat in air)
Keep **water away from electrical connections**
Use a low-voltage supply

core.h: Why water's high specific heat capacity matters
core.p: Because water needs a lot of energy to change its temperature, it can store and transfer large amounts of energy. This makes it useful in heating and cooling systems and affects the climate.
bullets: **Central heating** uses hot water to carry energy to radiators
**Car engine cooling systems** use water-based coolant to absorb energy
**Hot water bottles** stay warm for a long time
Coastal areas have **milder climates** because the sea warms and cools slowly
Storage heaters use materials with a **high c** (and high mass) to store energy overnight
Saucepans are made of metal (low c) so they **heat up quickly**

core.p: For the same mass and the same energy supplied, the temperature rise is inversely proportional to the specific heat capacity: Δθ = ΔE / (m c). Doubling c halves the temperature rise.
bullets: Same energy, same mass: **higher c means smaller Δθ**
Same energy, same c: **larger m means smaller Δθ**
Same mass, same Δθ: **energy needed is proportional to c**
Example: 4200 J warms 1 kg of water by 1 °C but would warm 1 kg of aluminium by about 4.7 °C

analogy.p: Think of temperature as the water level in a bucket and energy as the water you pour in. A material with a high specific heat capacity is like a very wide bucket: you have to pour in a lot of water (energy) to raise the level (temperature) by 1 cm. A low specific heat capacity material is a narrow bucket that fills up quickly. More mass is like having more buckets to fill side by side. Where it breaks down: a bucket's width is fixed by shape, while c comes from how a material's particles store energy, and the bucket picture says nothing about energy leaking to the surroundings or about changes of state.

terms.d: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C; unit J/kg°C.
The energy transferred to or from a system's thermal store, in joules.
Final temperature minus initial temperature, in °C.
The unit of energy.
Total kinetic and potential energy of the particles in a system.
A meter that measures the electrical energy transferred to a device, in joules.
An electrical heater placed inside a material or liquid to heat it.
Rate of energy transfer; P = E / t, measured in watts (W).
Measured with a voltmeter in parallel, in volts (V); used in P = V × I.
Measured with an ammeter in series, in amps (A).
Material that reduces the rate of energy transfer to the surroundings.
How well energy can pass between two objects; improved by filling gaps with water or oil.
Delay before a thermometer reaches the temperature of what it is measuring.
Slope of a graph; for temperature against energy it equals 1 / (m c).
An error that shifts all results the same way, such as energy loss making c too high.
Unpredictable variation in readings, reduced by repeating and averaging.

mistakes.w: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of a substance by 1 °C.
mistakes.r: It is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 °C.

mistakes.w: Substituting the final temperature for Δθ.
mistakes.r: Δθ = final temperature − initial temperature.

mistakes.w: Using mass in grams.
mistakes.r: Convert to kilograms before using ΔE = m c Δθ.

mistakes.w: Using time in minutes in E = P × t.
mistakes.r: Time must be in seconds.

mistakes.w: The value of c is too high because the thermometer was not accurate.
mistakes.r: Energy was transferred to the surroundings, so the temperature rise was smaller and c calculated too high.

mistakes.w: Insulation stops all energy loss.
mistakes.r: Insulation reduces the rate of energy transfer to the surroundings; it does not stop it.

mistakes.w: Using ΔE = m c Δθ while ice is melting.
mistakes.r: During a change of state temperature is constant; use specific latent heat instead.

mistakes.w: Unit of c written as J/kg or J/°C.
mistakes.r: The unit is J/kg°C.

exam.q: Define specific heat capacity.
model: Energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C
exam.tip: Must include both 1 kg and 1 °C.

exam.q: Calculate the energy needed to raise the temperature of 2.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 70 °C. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg°C.
exam.tip: Find Δθ first.

exam.q: A 0.50 kg copper block is given 3900 J of energy. c of copper = 390 J/kg°C. Calculate the temperature rise.
model: Δθ = ΔE / (m × c)
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting.

exam.q: Give the unit of specific heat capacity.
model: J/kg°C
exam.tip: J/kg K is also accepted.

exam.q: A 1.0 kg block is heated by a 50 W heater for 600 s and its temperature rises by 30 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of the block.
model: c = ΔE / (m × Δθ)
exam.tip: Two-step questions: find energy first.

exam.q: In PAG P5 a student finds a value of c for aluminium that is higher than the accepted value. Explain why.
model: Some energy from the heater is transferred to the surroundings / not to the block
So the temperature rise is smaller than expected, giving a larger value of c = ΔE / (m Δθ)
exam.tip: Explain the direction of the error.

exam.q: Suggest two improvements to reduce error in the specific heat capacity practical.
model: Wrap the block in insulation / add a lid
Put water or oil in the thermometer hole for better thermal contact (or record the highest temperature after switching off)
exam.tip: Each improvement should say what it does.

exam.q: Explain why water is used in central heating systems.
model: Water has a high specific heat capacity
So it can store / transfer a lot of energy for each degree its temperature changes
exam.tip: Link the property to the use.

exam.q: Water of mass 250 g cools from 80 °C to 30 °C. Calculate the energy transferred to the surroundings. c = 4200 J/kg°C.
exam.tip: Convert grams to kilograms.

exam.q: Describe how to determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block. Include the measurements you would make and how you would use them.
model: Measure the mass of the block on a balance
Insert an immersion heater and a thermometer (with water/oil in the hole); insulate the block
Record the initial temperature
Switch on the heater and measure the energy supplied with a joulemeter (or V, I and time, E = V I t)
Record the highest final temperature and calculate Δθ
Calculate c = ΔE / (m × Δθ), or plot temperature against energy and use c = 1 / (m × gradient)
exam.tip: Cover apparatus, measurements, calculation and error reduction in a logical order.

exam.q: Two blocks of equal mass, one aluminium (c = 900 J/kg°C) and one copper (c = 390 J/kg°C), receive the same energy. Which has the greater temperature rise? Explain.
model: Copper
Lower specific heat capacity, so less energy is needed per kg per °C; Δθ = ΔE / (m c) is larger
exam.tip: State the answer then justify with the equation.

worked.q: A kettle contains 1.5 kg of water at 15 °C. How much energy is needed to heat it to 100 °C? (c = 4200 J/kg°C)
steps: ΔE = m × c × Δθ

worked.q: PAG P5 results: a 1.0 kg aluminium block is heated by a heater with p.d. 12 V and current 4.0 A for 300 s. Its temperature rises from 20 °C to 36 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium.
steps: Energy supplied: E = V × I × t = 12 × 4.0 × 300 = 14 400 J
c = 900 J/kg°C

worked.q: A 0.20 kg block of copper at 25 °C is given 1560 J of energy. c = 390 J/kg°C. Find its final temperature.
steps: Δθ = ΔE / (m × c)
Δθ = 20 °C
Final temperature = 25 + 20 = 45 °C

phy_ocra.1.3.summary: When a substance changes state (melts, freezes, boils, condenses), energy is transferred to or from its internal energy store but its temperature stays constant, because the energy is used to break or form the bonds between particles rather than to speed them up. The **specific latent heat** of a substance is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of it without a change in temperature. You must be able to use energy for a change of state = mass x specific latent heat (E = mL), distinguish it clearly from specific heat capacity, interpret heating and cooling curves, and describe how to measure it in PAG P5.

core.p: During a change of state, energy is still being transferred to (or from) the substance, but the thermometer reading does not change. This 'hidden' energy is called **latent heat** (latent means hidden). It changes the **potential energy** of the particles (the energy stored in the forces/bonds between them), not their **kinetic energy**, so the temperature stays the same.
bullets: Temperature is linked to the **average kinetic energy** of the particles.
During melting and boiling, energy goes into **breaking intermolecular bonds** (overcoming forces of attraction), increasing potential energy.
During freezing and condensing, bonds **form** and energy is **released** to the surroundings.
Because kinetic energy does not change, the **temperature stays constant** during the whole change of state.
The **internal energy** (total kinetic + potential energy of the particles) still increases when melting or boiling.

callouts.p: During any change of state the temperature stays constant even though energy is being transferred: the energy changes the internal energy (potential energy of particles), not the temperature.

core.p: The **specific latent heat (L)** of a substance is the amount of energy needed to change the state of **1 kg** of the substance **with no change in temperature**. Every substance has its own value, and each substance has a different value for melting and for boiling.
bullets: Unit: **joules per kilogram, J/kg** (often given as kJ/kg or MJ/kg).
'Specific' means **per kilogram**.
The same amount of energy is **released** when 1 kg changes back (freezes or condenses).
It is a property of the **material**, not of the particular sample.

callouts.p: The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature.

core.p: There are two specific latent heats for each substance, depending on which change of state happens.
bullets: **Specific latent heat of fusion**: energy to change 1 kg from **solid to liquid** (melting) at constant temperature. Same energy released on freezing.
**Specific latent heat of vaporisation**: energy to change 1 kg from **liquid to gas** (boiling) at constant temperature. Same energy released on condensing.
For water: L of fusion is about **334 000 J/kg**; L of vaporisation is about **2 260 000 J/kg**.
Vaporisation is much larger because the particles must be **completely separated** and pushed far apart against the atmosphere, whereas melting only loosens the fixed arrangement.

head: Quantity
Change of state
Water value
rows: Solid to liquid (melting) / liquid to solid (freezing)
Liquid to gas (boiling) / gas to liquid (condensing)

callouts.p: Remember 'fusion' as 'fuse' in a fuse that melts. Vaporisation = turning into vapour.

core.p: The energy needed for a change of state depends on how much substance there is and on what it is made of. OCR gives this as: **thermal energy for a change in state (J) = mass (kg) x specific latent heat (J/kg)**.
bullets: **E = m x L**
E = energy in **joules (J)**
m = mass in **kilograms (kg)**
L = specific latent heat in **J/kg**
Rearranged: **L = E / m** and **m = E / L**.
There is **no temperature change** in this equation, unlike the specific heat capacity equation.

callouts.p: Thermal energy for a change in state = mass x specific latent heat. Learn it; you must recall and apply it.
Convert grams to kilograms (divide by 1000) and kJ to J (multiply by 1000) before substituting.

core.p: A **heating curve** is a graph of temperature against time for a substance being heated at a steady rate. It has sloping sections, where temperature rises, and **flat sections (plateaus)** where the substance changes state.
bullets: Sloping sections: energy increases the **kinetic energy** of particles, so temperature rises (use E = m c delta T).
First flat section: **melting point**; solid and liquid present together; energy = m x L of fusion.
Second flat section: **boiling point**; liquid and gas present; energy = m x L of vaporisation.
The boiling plateau is **longer** than the melting plateau because L of vaporisation is bigger, so it takes longer at the same power.
The **gradient** of sloping parts depends on specific heat capacity: a smaller gradient means a larger c for that state.

callouts.p: If you are asked what is happening on a flat part, say: the substance is changing state, energy is breaking bonds, the temperature stays constant.

fig.cap: Heating curve for water heated at a steady rate. The temperature rises on sloping sections and stays constant on the flat sections, where energy is used to change state (melting at 0 C, boiling at 100 C). The boiling plateau is longer because the specific latent heat of vaporisation is larger.

core.p: A **cooling curve** is the reverse: temperature against time as a substance cools. The flat sections show where the substance **condenses** or **freezes**.
bullets: Flat sections occur at the **same temperatures** as on the heating curve (boiling point = condensing point; melting point = freezing point).
During the plateau, bonds are **forming** and energy is **released** to the surroundings, which keeps the temperature constant even though the substance is losing energy.
Energy released = m x L, using the same L as for the forward change.
This is why a freezing liquid stays at its freezing point until it is all solid.

callouts.p: On a plateau the substance is still transferring energy. Do not write 'no energy is transferred'.

core.p: Use the particle model to explain WHY the temperature does not change. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles; a change of state changes the arrangement and the potential energy instead.
bullets: Solid: particles in a **fixed, regular arrangement**, vibrating about fixed positions, strong forces of attraction.
Melting: energy overcomes **some** of the forces, so particles can slide past each other.
Liquid to gas: energy overcomes **all** the forces, so particles separate completely and move far apart at random.
Kinetic energy (speed) stays the same during the change, so **temperature is constant**.
Potential energy increases, so **internal energy increases**.

core.h: Specific heat capacity vs specific latent heat
core.p: The spec requires you to **distinguish** between these two. Both are energy per kilogram, but they describe different things.
bullets: **Specific heat capacity (c)**: energy to raise the temperature of 1 kg by 1 C; temperature **changes**, state does **not**.
**Specific latent heat (L)**: energy to change the state of 1 kg; state **changes**, temperature does **not**.
c is used on the **sloping** parts of a heating curve; L on the **flat** parts.
c has units **J/kg C**; L has units **J/kg**.
To heat ice at -10 C to steam at 100 C you need **both** equations, added together.

callouts.p: If the unit has a degree symbol it is specific heat capacity; specific latent heat is just J/kg.

core.p: Harder questions combine both ideas, for example heating water from room temperature and then boiling it. Treat each stage separately and **add** the energies.
bullets: Stage 1 (warm the solid or liquid): E1 = m c delta T.
Stage 2 (change state): E2 = m L.
Total energy = E1 + E2 (+ further stages).
Use the correct c for each state (ice, water and steam all have different values).
If power and time are involved: **E = P x t**, so time = E / P.

callouts.p: An electric heater transfers E = P t. Combine with E = mL to find L = P t / m.

core.h: PAG P5: measuring specific latent heat
core.p: In PAG P5 you determine a specific latent heat experimentally. For fusion of ice, crushed ice is melted with an **electric immersion heater** and the energy supplied and mass melted are measured.
bullets: Place crushed ice in a **funnel** above a beaker, with an immersion heater in the ice.
Set up an **identical control funnel** with no heater (or heater off) to measure ice melted by the room alone.
Switch on the heater; measure energy with a **joulemeter**, or with an **ammeter, voltmeter and stopclock** (E = V I t).
Collect the meltwater for a fixed time; find its mass with a **balance**.
Subtract the mass melted in the control funnel from the mass melted in the heated funnel.
Calculate **L = E / m**.
For vaporisation: boil water in a beaker on a balance with a heater; measure the mass lost as steam while water is already boiling and the energy supplied.

callouts.p: Ice also melts from energy absorbed from the warmer room. The control lets you subtract this so m is only the mass melted by the heater.

core.p: Real experiments give values that differ from data-book values. You should explain the sources of error and how to reduce them.
bullets: Energy is transferred to or from the **surroundings**, so not all heater energy melts the ice (or the room melts extra ice).
Using **crushed ice** gives better contact with the heater.
Ice should be at **0 C** (melting) before starting, so energy only changes state and does not warm the ice.
Water left clinging to ice or funnel is not collected, so m is too small and L too large.
Insulate the apparatus; use a control; repeat and calculate a mean.
In boiling experiments, start timing only once the water is **already boiling**, and steam condensing back reduces the mass lost.

callouts.p: Say the direction: if energy is lost to the surroundings, E is overestimated for the mass changed, so the calculated L is too high.

core.p: Latent heat explains many everyday effects, which can appear as 'explain' questions.
bullets: **Sweating**: evaporating sweat takes latent heat of vaporisation from the skin, cooling you.
**Steam burns** are worse than burns from boiling water at 100 C, because condensing steam releases a large amount of latent heat onto the skin.
**Ice in drinks** cools them well because melting ice absorbs latent heat of fusion.
**Refrigerators** use a refrigerant that evaporates inside (absorbing energy) and condenses outside (releasing energy).
Mass is **conserved** during changes of state; only the energy and arrangement of particles change.

analogy.p: Imagine a crowd walking towards a stadium. Their walking speed is like temperature. At the ticket barrier everyone has to stop and pay (the latent heat) to get through; while they are paying, nobody speeds up, so the 'temperature' is constant, but money (energy) is still being handed over. The bigger barrier into the stadium itself (vaporisation) costs much more than the first gate (fusion). Where it breaks down: in reality particles do not stop moving during a change of state, they keep the same average kinetic energy, and the energy goes into separating particles rather than being 'spent' and gone; it is stored as potential energy and given back when the substance condenses or freezes.

mistakes.w: The temperature stays the same because no energy is being transferred.
mistakes.r: Energy is still transferred, but it changes the potential energy (breaks bonds), not the kinetic energy, so temperature is constant.

mistakes.w: Specific latent heat is the energy to raise 1 kg by 1 C.
mistakes.r: That is specific heat capacity; specific latent heat is the energy to change the state of 1 kg with no temperature change.

mistakes.w: Using grams for mass in E = mL.
mistakes.r: Mass must be in kg, so 250 g = 0.25 kg.

mistakes.w: Giving the unit of L as J/kg C.
mistakes.r: Specific latent heat is in J/kg.

mistakes.w: Using L of fusion for boiling.
mistakes.r: Boiling and condensing use the specific latent heat of vaporisation.

mistakes.w: The particles speed up during melting.
mistakes.r: The average kinetic energy is constant; forces between particles are overcome and potential energy increases.

mistakes.w: Only adding the latent heat in a two-stage question.
mistakes.r: Calculate m c delta T for the temperature rise and m L for the change of state, then add.

mistakes.w: The ice melts so energy is destroyed.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred to the internal energy store; it is conserved and released again on freezing.

exam.q: Define specific latent heat.
model: Energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance
with no change in temperature
exam.tip: Both '1 kg' and 'no temperature change' are needed for full marks.

exam.q: State the unit of specific latent heat.
model: J/kg
exam.tip: No degree symbol.

exam.q: Calculate the energy needed to melt 0.50 kg of ice at 0 C. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 334 000 J/kg.
exam.tip: Write the equation first; it often earns a mark.

exam.q: A heater supplies 452 000 J to boiling water and 0.20 kg of water turns to steam. Calculate the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water.
model: L = E / m
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting.

exam.q: Explain why the temperature of water stays at 100 C while it boils, even though it is still being heated.
model: Energy is used to break bonds / overcome forces between particles
This increases potential energy (internal energy) of particles
Kinetic energy of particles does not increase, so temperature is constant
exam.tip: Link temperature to kinetic energy.

exam.q: Explain the difference between specific heat capacity and specific latent heat.
model: Specific heat capacity is energy to raise temperature of 1 kg by 1 C
Specific heat capacity involves a temperature change with no change of state
Specific latent heat is energy to change state of 1 kg
Specific latent heat involves no temperature change
exam.tip: Make a direct comparison for each feature.

exam.q: Explain why a scald from steam at 100 C is more serious than a scald from water at 100 C.
model: Steam condenses on the skin
Releasing the latent heat of vaporisation
So much more energy is transferred to the skin (as well as cooling of the water)
exam.tip: Use the word 'condenses'.

exam.q: Calculate the mass of ice that melts when 66 800 J is supplied. L of fusion = 334 000 J/kg.
exam.tip: Check units: J divided by J/kg gives kg.

exam.q: Describe how to measure the specific latent heat of fusion of ice in the laboratory. Include how you would make your result accurate.
model: Put crushed ice at 0 C in a funnel with an immersion heater, beaker below
Set up an identical control funnel without the heater turned on
Measure energy supplied with a joulemeter (or V, I and time, E = V I t)
Collect and measure mass of meltwater on a balance for both funnels over the same time
Subtract control mass from heated mass
Calculate L = E / m; repeat and take a mean; insulate to reduce energy transfer from surroundings
exam.tip: Give a clear, logical sequence and include the calculation.

exam.q: A 2.0 kW kettle contains 0.50 kg of water already at 100 C. How long does it take to boil away 0.10 kg of water? L of vaporisation = 2 260 000 J/kg.
exam.tip: Convert kW to W.

exam.q: On a heating curve, explain why the plateau at the boiling point is longer than the plateau at the melting point.
model: Specific latent heat of vaporisation is larger than of fusion
So more energy, and so more time at the same power, is needed to boil than to melt the same mass
exam.tip: Refer to the same rate of heating.

worked.q: How much energy is needed to turn 250 g of water at 100 C into steam at 100 C? L of vaporisation of water = 2 260 000 J/kg.
steps: Convert mass: 250 g = 0.250 kg
Equation: E = m L
Substitute: E = 0.250 x 2 260 000

worked.q: In a PAG P5 experiment a joulemeter reads 24 000 J. 0.085 kg of meltwater is collected from the heated funnel and 0.013 kg from the control funnel in the same time. Calculate the specific latent heat of fusion of ice.
steps: Mass melted by the heater = 0.085 - 0.013 = 0.072 kg
L = E / m
L = 333 333 J/kg, about 333 000 J/kg

worked.q: Calculate the total energy needed to turn 0.40 kg of ice at 0 C into water at 20 C. L of fusion = 334 000 J/kg; c of water = 4200 J/kg C.
steps: Stage 2, warm: E2 = m c delta T = 0.40 x 4200 x 20 = 33 600 J
